title: Client Prefetch Stub and Cost Sensitivity Cheatsheet
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary
This page is a compact reference for engineers integrating Redwood SDKs who want an opinionated, low-friction pattern for local testing (stubbed runtime), client-side prefetch/prediction batching, and cost-sensitive request shaping. It combines a short quickstart, recommended configuration table, canonical fixes for common support issues, and an on-call checklist for shipping safely.

When to use this cheatsheet
- Building or iterating an LLM-backed feature locally where full runtime access is slow or costly.
- Prototyping client-side batching or prefetch strategies before server rollout.
- Validating cost vs. latency tradeoffs with offline traces.

Goals
- Provide a reproducible local stub pattern that mirrors Redwood routing semantics.
- Offer a narrow set of batching/prefetch defaults with clear cost and latency tradeoffs.
- List deterministic troubleshooting steps (canonical fixes) for the top 6 support patterns we see.

Quickstart: local stub + prefetch loop (5 steps)
1) Install local stub CLI and runtime shim
   - Linux/macOS: pip install redwood-runtime-stub==0.2.1 or use the prebuilt docker image redwood/stub:0.2.1
   - Start a stub that accepts the same HTTP/JSON surface as hosted API for generation + embeddings:

     ```bash
     # Docker (recommended):
     docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -e REDWOOD_STUB_MODE=prefetch redwood/stub:0.2.1

     # Python CLI (dev):
     redwood-stub serve --port 8080 --mode prefetch --cache-size 500
     ```

2) Wire SDK to local endpoint (example Node.js)
   - Set endpoint override in environment for local dev only:

     ```js
     // process.env.REDWOOD_API_URL = 'http://localhost:8080/v1'
     import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood/inference-js';
     const client = new RedwoodClient({ baseUrl: process.env.REDWOOD_API_URL });
     ```

3) Add a simple prefetch + bundling layer in the client
   - Strategy: collect similar prompts for 50ms window, then issue a batched request. Keep max bundle size = 8 unless latency SLO allows higher.

     ```js
     // pseudo-code: bundler.js
     const queue = [];
     function request(modelInput) {
       return new Promise((resolve) => {
         queue.push({ modelInput, resolve });
       });
     }
     setInterval(async () => {
       if (!queue.length) return;
       const batch = queue.splice(0, 8);
       const response = await client.generate({ model: 'redwood-alpha', inputs: batch.map(b=>b.modelInput) });
       response.forEach((r,i)=> batch[i].resolve(r));
     }, 50);
     ```

4) Enable cache hints and KV prefixing on the stub for realistic behavior
   - The stub includes a switch that simulates prefix/KV cache hits. Turn on using REDWOOD_STUB_CACHE_HINTS=1. This will let you test eviction behavior locally.

5) Run trace-driven cost sensitivity tests
   - Replay a 10k request trace against the stub, measure tokens and latency, and tune bundle window and max size until you hit target token/unit cost or latency. Use the provided trace-replayer: redwood-stub replay --trace example-trace.json --metrics out.csv

Recommended parameter table (opinionated defaults)
| Parameter | Default | When to increase | Expected cost impact | Expected latency impact | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| bundle_window_ms | 50 | When requests are bursty and SLO allows +20ms | lowers per-token cost via batching | +10–+60ms tail latency | Good starting point for web UX features |
| max_bundle_size | 8 | For high-throughput background jobs | reduces calls & per-call overhead | may increase median latency if window grows | Keep <= 32 for general purpose |
| prefetch_lookahead_tokens | 64 | For completion-heavy prompts where next-token distribution is predictable | modest increase if predictions wrong | reduces latency on hit | Use in product flows with strong user-action priors |
| cache_ttl_seconds | 300 | When results are stable (e.g., embeddings) | large savings for repeated queries | none on hit; misses cost same | Use longer TTLs for idempotent outputs |
| kv_cache_max_entries | 5_000 | Large conversational workloads | big savings for repeated prefixes | small memory cost | Evaluate on representative trace |

Cost/latency tradeoff guidance
- If 95th pct latency increases > 150ms after raising bundle_window_ms, reduce window or lower max_bundle_size.
- If per-request cost (tokens billed) exceeds projection by >10%, enable prefix hashing to increase cache hit rates.
- For interactive UIs, prefer bundle_window_ms <= 50 and max_bundle_size <= 8. For batch jobs, you can push both higher.

Canonical fixes for top support patterns
1) Symptom: Local responses are faster than hosted but production shows high variance
   - Fix: Confirm production routing policy is routing to the same model family and not falling back. Check /api/v1/routing/debug for active policies. Add a traffic mirror to the stub to compare payloads.
2) Symptom: Stubbing shows consistent cache hits, but production misses frequently
   - Fix: Ensure request fingerprinting (prompt normalization + tenant-scoped key) matches production. Production includes tenant_id and model_version in the cache key; stub uses a simplified key unless REDWOOD_STUB_FULL_KEY=1. Turn it on to replicate misses.
3) Symptom: Batches sometimes split identical prompts into different calls
   - Fix: Confirm bundler groups by fingerprint canonicalization (strip timestamps, IDs). Add a deterministic sort step before batching.
4) Symptom: Observed token usage > expected after enabling prefetch
   - Fix: Reduce prefetch_lookahead_tokens, and use conservative prefetching profiles per model. Run A/B test with sampled traffic to measure delta.
5) Symptom: Intermittent 429s from stub during replay tests
   - Fix: Increase stub's simulated capacity (REDWOOD_STUB_SIMULATED_TPS) or reduce bundle concurrency. For production 429s, check rate-limit headers from Redwood API and back off exponentially.
6) Symptom: Local trace replay mismatches production outputs
   - Fix: Ensure model_version pins are identical and that quantization profiles are compatible; the stub defaults to the float32 path unless REDWOOD_STUB_QUANTIZED=1 is set.

Observability checklist (for SDK integrations)
- Instrument: request_id, tenant_id, model_version, prompt_fingerprint, bundle_size, latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, cache_hit (bool).
- Dashboards: per-route token cost, bundle_size distribution, cache hit rate, and 95/99 latency.
- Alerts: cache_hit_rate < 5% for 1h; median bundle_size < 1 for feature routes; 95 latency degradation >20% week-over-week.

Rollout checklist (safe progression)
1) Smoke in sandbox with stub: run 10k synthetic requests, validate outputs and metrics.
2) Canary 1% on hosted: enable canary routing to dedicated canary pool, collect 24h of telemetry.
3) Canary 10%: expand if metrics within thresholds. 48h telemetry.
4) Gradual ramp to 100% with monitoring playbook active and an automatic fallback to single-request, low-batch mode.

Appendix: small sample trace JSON (3 entries)
```json
[ 
  {"tenant_id":"team-123","model":"redwood-alpha","input":"Summarize: The Q4 roadmap includes...","timestamp":1650000000},
  {"tenant_id":"team-123","model":"redwood-alpha","input":"Summarize: The Q4 roadmap includes...","timestamp":1650000001},
  {"tenant_id":"team-456","model":"redwood-alpha","input":"Extract keywords: machine learning, inference","timestamp":1650000003}
]
```

Notes and rationale
- The bundling defaults balance web UX latency against unit-cost reduction and were calibrated against production traces from marketing site search and in-product suggestions.
- The stub intentionally offers toggles (full key mode, quantized path, simulated TPS) so teams can reproduce a range of production phenomena without full infra access.

If you have questions or want a pairing session to run your trace against the stub, open a ticket with tag "devx-stub-support" and reach out to any reviewer.
